summary: Specifies the MTU and frame format for sending IPv6 packets over Token Ring networks. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2470 says how to send IPv6 packets over a Token Ring network. It gives the frame layout, the largest packet to use, the way to build an IPv6 address from the hardware address, and how IPv6 group addresses are turned into Token Ring functional addresses.

subtitle: How to carry IPv6 packets on IEEE 802.5 Token Ring, from the frame layout to the link-local address.

tldr.problem: IPv6 needs a defined way to travel over every kind of link, and Token Ring was not covered. Without one, an IPv6 node on a Token Ring network would not know the frame layout, the packet size to use, or how to form its link-local address.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC specifies the MTU rules, the LLC/SNAP frame format with the EtherType for IPv6, the interface identifier derived from the Token Ring hardware address, the link-local address, and the mapping of IPv6 unicast and multicast addresses onto Token Ring addresses.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2470 is a Proposed Standard from December 1998 and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 2470 is a Proposed Standard published in December 1998 and has not been obsoleted. It defines how IPv6 is carried on IEEE 802.5 Token Ring networks.

sections.title: What the RFC Specifies
sections.content:
RFC 2470 covers four things: the maximum transmission unit (MTU) and the frame format for sending IPv6 packets on Token Ring, the method for forming IPv6 link-local addresses on Token Ring, and the content of the Source/Target Link-layer Address option used in Router Solicitation, Router Advertisement, Redirect, Neighbor Solicitation and Neighbor Advertisement messages when those messages travel over Token Ring.

The RFC carries one warning that implementers are told to note carefully. Token Ring adaptors assume addresses are in non-canonical rather than canonical bit order, so special care has to be taken to make sure addresses are processed correctly. The RFC points to RFC 2469 for the details.

The scope is deliberately narrow. It is about IPv6 on one particular link technology, and it leans on the general IPv6 specifications for addressing and neighbour discovery rather than repeating them.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC fixes the details that a Token Ring network needs for IPv6: the frame layout, the packet size, the address format and the neighbour discovery option. It also warns that Token Ring hardware uses a different bit order for addresses than most other technologies.

sections.title: Maximum Transmission Unit
sections.content:
An IEEE 802.5 network has no single maximum frame size. The size depends on how long a node may hold the token, which in turn depends on the data signalling rate and the number of nodes on the ring. Implementations must therefore rely on manual configuration or on router advertisements to learn the real sizes. Common defaults are approximately 2000, 4000 and 8000 octets.

Where nothing else is known, an implementation should use a default MTU of 1500 octets, because that size works with all the common 802.5 defaults and with Ethernet LANs in a bridged environment. In a source route bridged network, the largest frame subfield of the routing information field gives the size for a particular path. Because the LLC header is always 8 octets long for IPv6, the IPv6 MTU is the largest frame size minus 8. An implementation that works this way must keep a separate MTU for each neighbour.

The RFC tabulates the common values. Some of the 802.1D largest frame values give an IP MTU below 1280 bytes, which is the IPv6 minimum, and communication across such a path is generally not possible with IPv6.

When several sources disagree, the RFC sets the order of preference. Largest frame values from source route bridging come first, but only for specific unicast destinations and only if they are not greater than a value from router advertisements. Router advertisements come next, but only if not greater than any manual configuration, including DHCP. Manual configuration comes third, and the default of 1500 comes last.
sections.plainLanguage: Token Ring has no fixed maximum frame size, so the size has to be learned or configured. The default to use is 1500 octets, and when sources disagree the RFC says which one wins: a source route bridge first, then a router advertisement, then a manual setting, and the default last.

sections.title: The Token Ring Frame Format
sections.content:
IPv6 packets travel in LLC/SNAP frames, and the data field holds the IPv6 header and payload. The frame starts with the Starting Delimiter, the Access Control and the Frame Control fields, followed by the 48-bit IEEE destination address and the 48-bit IEEE source address. After that come the LLC/SNAP fields: the Destination Service Access Point, the Source Service Access Point, the Control Field, the Organizationally Unique Identifier and the EtherType. The frame ends with the Frame Check Sequence, the Ending Delimiter and the Frame Status.

Several of those fields carry fixed values. For the LLC/SNAP format the DSAP and SSAP shall always contain the value 0xAA, the Control Field shall always contain 0x03 for Unnumbered Information, the OUI shall always contain 0x000000 for EtherType encoding, and the EtherType shall always contain 0x86DD for IPv6.

Where source route bridges are present, a routing information field may follow the source address. It is present when the most significant bit of the source address is set, and it holds a two-octet Routing Control header followed by up to seven two-octet Route Designator fields. The Routing Control carries a broadcast indicator, the length of the field, a direction bit and the largest frame value. On transmission, the Route Designator fields give the sequence of bridge and LAN segment numbers the packet is to traverse, and it is the sender's job to supply that sequence for unicast datagrams.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv6 packets are carried in LLC/SNAP frames with fixed values in the header fields and the EtherType 0x86DD. When source route bridges are present, the frame also carries the list of bridges and segments the packet has to pass through.

sections.title: Interface Identifiers and the Link-Local Address
sections.content:
The IPv6 interface identifier for a Token Ring interface is built from the EUI-64 identifier derived from the interface's built-in 48-bit IEEE 802 address. The first three octets of the Token Ring address, the OUI, become the first three octets of the EUI-64, the fourth and fifth octets of the EUI are set to the fixed value FFFE in hexadecimal, and the last three octets of the Token Ring address become the last three octets of the EUI-64.

The interface identifier is then formed by complementing the Universal/Local bit, the next-to-lowest-order bit of the first octet of the EUI-64. Complementing that bit generally changes a 0 into a 1, because a built-in address is expected to come from the universally administered address space, where a 0 in that position means globally unique. A globally unique IPv6 interface identifier is signalled by a 1 in the corresponding position. As an example, the built-in address 34-56-78-9A-BC-DE gives the interface identifier 36-56-78-FF-FE-9A-BC-DE.

A MAC address set manually or by software should not be used to derive the interface identifier. If such an address has to be used, its global uniqueness should be reflected in the value of the U/L bit. Any IPv6 address prefix used for stateless autoconfiguration of a Token Ring interface must be 64 bits long.

The link-local address is formed by appending the interface identifier to the prefix FE80::/64. The prefix is ten bits of 1111111010, then 54 zero bits, then the 64-bit interface identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: The interface identifier comes from the interface's own hardware address: the first three bytes are kept, two fixed bytes are inserted, the last three are kept, and one bit is flipped to mark the address as unique. The link-local address is that identifier placed after the fixed prefix FE80::/64.

sections.title: Unicast Address Mapping
sections.content:
The general procedure for mapping unicast IPv6 addresses into link-layer addresses is described in the IPv6 neighbour discovery specification. What this RFC adds is the form the Source/Target Link-layer Address option takes on Token Ring.

The option has a Type field, where 1 means a source link-layer address and 2 means a target link-layer address, a Length field of 1 in units of 8 octets, and the Token Ring address itself: the 48-bit IEEE 802 address in canonical bit order. It is the address the interface currently responds to, which may differ from the built-in address used to derive the interface identifier.

Where source routing bridges are used, the source route for the path to a destination can be extracted from the routing information field of received Neighbor Advertisement messages. The field of a received packet can be turned back into a source route for sending return traffic by toggling the direction bit and making sure the broadcast field shows a Specifically Routed Frame.
sections.plainLanguage: Neighbour discovery messages carry the link-layer address of the sender or the target. On Token Ring that address is the 48-bit hardware address, and the RFC also explains how to recover the route back from a received frame.

sections.title: Multicast Address Mapping
sections.content:
All IPv6 packets with a multicast destination address are sent to Token Ring functional addresses. The RFC gives the mapping. The functional address 03-00-80-00-00-00 carries the All-Nodes addresses and the solicited-node addresses. The functional address 03-00-40-00-00-00 carries the All-Routers addresses. Every other multicast address is mapped by its three least significant bits: 000, 001, 010, 011, 100, 101, 110 and 111 each have their own functional address, with the low bit of the third octet set accordingly.

The RFC notes that other protocols may use these same functional addresses, so a frame sent to one of them is not guaranteed to carry an IPv6 datagram.

In a bridged Token Ring network, all multicast packets should be sent with a routing information field that specifies the use of the Spanning Tree Explorer. Some very old bridge implementations are believed not to support that mechanism properly, and in such environments multicast traffic sent through bridges must use a routing information field with the All Routes Explorer. An implementation may therefore want to allow IP multicast traffic to be sent with the All Routes Explorer, but that ability must be configurable by a system administrator, and the default setting of the switch must be to use the Spanning Tree Explorer.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv6 group addresses are sent to fixed Token Ring functional addresses: one for all nodes, one for all routers, and eight more chosen by the low bits of the group address. Multicast frames crossing bridges need a route field, and the RFC says which explorer to use.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Token Ring, like most broadcast LAN technologies, has inherent security weaknesses. Any sender on the ring can claim the identity of another and forge traffic. The RFC states that it is the responsibility of the higher layers to take appropriate steps in environments where such weaknesses are unacceptable.
sections.plainLanguage: Any station on a Token Ring can send frames that pretend to come from someone else. The RFC leaves the protection against that to the layers above, such as the security mechanisms built into IPv6.

fields.name: Destination Address
fields.desc: 48-bit IEEE address of the destination station.

fields.name: Source Address
fields.desc: 48-bit IEEE address of the source station.

fields.name: DSAP
fields.desc: Destination Service Access Point. Always 0xAA in LLC/SNAP format.

fields.name: SSAP
fields.desc: Source Service Access Point. Always 0xAA in LLC/SNAP format.

fields.name: CTL
fields.desc: Control Field. Always 0x03 for Unnumbered Information.

fields.name: OUI
fields.desc: Organizationally Unique Identifier. Always 0x000000 for EtherType encoding.

fields.name: EtherType
fields.desc: Protocol type of the encapsulated payload. Always 0x86DD for IPv6.

items.title: 1. Source route bridging
items.text: Largest frame values, for specific unicast destinations only.

items.title: 2. Router advertisements
items.text: Used only if not greater than any manual configuration.

items.title: 4. Default
items.text: 1500 octets, when nothing else is known.
